claim: Observing and interpreting social interactions of other individuals is crucial for our everyday life.
source: Observing and interpreting social interactions of other individuals is crucial for our everyday life.
evidence: This is a general statement about human social cognition presented as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Primates can readily recognize social interactions such as play, fight, and grooming of other group members.
source: We share this remarkable ability with other primates that can also readily recognize social interactions such as play, fight, and grooming of other group members (Ambady et al., 2000; Ebenau et al., 2019; Spelke and Kinzler, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research on primate social cognition.

claim: Monkeys use information from observing social interactions to infer social hierarchies, adjust their behavior, and find allies.
source: Monkeys use this information to infer social hierarchies, adjust their behavior, and find allies (Bergman et al., 2003; Cheney et al., 1986).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research on monkey social behavior.

claim: In Old World macaque monkeys, areas in parietal and frontal cortex were exclusively activated by the observation of social interactions of other macaques.
source: In Old World macaque monkeys, Sliwa and Freiwald, 2017 recently identified areas in parietal and frontal cortex that were exclusively activated by the observation of social interactions of other macaques using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI).
evidence: Supported by citation to a specific fMRI study in macaques.

claim: The social interaction network in macaques resembles the human default mode network.
source: Interestingly, this network in macaques resembles the human default mode network (Mars et al., 2012) and the theory of mind network (Gallagher and Frith, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations comparing macaque and human brain networks.

claim: The social interaction network may play a key role in the human default mode network and theory of mind network and be a conserved feature across primates.
source: As these networks share anatomical and functional characteristics, it suggests that the social interaction network may play a key role in these two human networks and be a conserved feature across primates (Sliwa and Freiwald, 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on network similarities, supported by citation.

claim: Macaque monkeys may not be an ideal nonhuman primate model for studying the neural basis of social cognition due to their size and aggression toward conspecifics.
source: Although macaque monkeys are widely used to study the neural basis of higher cognitive function, they may not be an ideal nonhuman primate model for studying the neural basis of social cognition as laboratory studies of social behavior are challenging due to their size and aggression toward conspecifics.
evidence: This is a reasoned argument based on practical considerations of working with macaques.

claim: Different species of macaques display varying types of prosociality but no cooperative breeding.
source: Different species of macaques display varying type of prosociality but no cooperative breeding (Balasubramaniam et al., 2018; Ballesta and Duhamel, 2015; Beisner et al., 2016; de Waal, 1986; Joly et al., 2017; McCowan et al., 2011; Thierry et al., 2000)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to research on macaque social behavior.

claim: Pairing and matching more than two macaque monkeys is often difficult under laboratory conditions.
source: However, pairing and matching more than two macaque monkeys is often difficult under laboratory conditions.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about working with macaques in laboratory settings.

claim: The common marmoset lives in family groups and shares certain similarities with humans such as prosocial behavior, social cognition, and cooperative breeding.
source: For these reasons, the common marmoset (Callithrix jacchus), a small New World nonhuman primate species that lives in family groups and shares certain similarities with humans such as prosocial behavior, social cognition (Burkart and Finkenwirth, 2015; Miller et al., 2016), and cooperative breeding (Burkart et al., 2009; Caselli et al., 2018), has garnered interest as a powerful primate model for human social behavior (Huang et al., 2020; Miller et al., 2016; Saito, 2015; Yokoyama et al., 2013; Yokoyama and Onoe, 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to research on marmoset social behavior and cognition.

claim: The common marmoset has garnered interest as a powerful primate model for human social behavior.
source: For these reasons, the common marmoset (Callithrix jacchus), a small New World nonhuman primate species that lives in family groups and shares certain similarities with humans such as prosocial behavior, social cognition (Burkart and Finkenwirth, 2015; Miller et al., 2016), and cooperative breeding (Burkart et al., 2009; Caselli et al., 2018), has garnered interest as a powerful primate model for human social behavior (Huang et al., 2020; Miller et al., 2016; Saito, 2015; Yokoyama et al., 2013; Yokoyama and Onoe, 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to research on marmosets as models for human behavior.

claim: The study used ultra-high-field (9.4 T) fMRI in fully awake marmosets to identify neural circuits involved in social interaction observation.
source: Here, we aimed to identify the neural circuits involved in social interaction observation in marmosets using ultra-high-field (9.4 T) fMRI in fully awake animals.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the current study.

claim: The study acquired fMRI data from marmosets while they viewed videos of two marmosets interacting with each other (social condition) or of two marmosets engaged in independent goal-directed behavior (nonsocial condition).
source: Similar to Sliwa and Freiwald's study (2017), we acquired fMRI data from marmosets while they viewed videos of two marmosets interacting with each other (social condition) or of two marmosets engaged in independent goal-directed behavior (nonsocial condition).
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the current study.

claim: Three common marmosets were scanned, and eight runs per marmoset were used for group analysis (24 runs in total).
source: Three common marmosets were scanned, and eight runs per marmosets were used for group analysis (24 runs in total).
evidence: This describes the sample size and data collection for the study.

claim: In the social conditions, the actions performed in the videos included eating, playing, fighting, and grooming between two marmosets.
source: In the social conditions, the actions performed in the videos included eating, playing, fighting, and grooming between two marmosets.
evidence: This describes the stimuli used in the social condition.

claim: In the nonsocial conditions, the actions performed in the videos included eating, exploring objects, looking around, and scratching.
source: In the nonsocial conditions, the actions performed in the videos included eating, exploring objects, looking around, and scratching.
evidence: This describes the stimuli used in the nonsocial condition.

claim: Both social and nonsocial videos activated a large network including visual, temporal, parietal, and frontal areas.
source: Both social (Figure 1a) and nonsocial (Figure 1c) videos activated a large network including visual (V1, V2, V3, V4, V4T, V6, V6A, 19M, MT), temporal (FST, TE1, TE2, TE3, TEO, IPa), parietal (MIP, VIP, LIP, AIP, PGM), and frontal areas (45, 47L, 46v, 10, 8av, 8ad, 8C, 6DR).
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The scrambled versions of social and nonsocial videos showed strong activation in visual and temporal areas.
source: The scrambled versions (Figure 1b, d) showed strong activation in visual (V1, V2, V3, V4, V4T, MT) and temporal areas (FST, TEO, IPa).
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The scrambled versions also showed activations in frontal cortex areas 47L, 45, and 8av.
source: Activations were also found in frontal cortex (47L, 45, 8av).
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI data from scrambled conditions.

claim: The scrambled version of the nonsocial condition also showed activation in S2E, 1/2, 3a, 3b.
source: The scrambled version of the nonsocial condition (Figure 1d) also showed activation in S2E, 1/2, 3a, 3b.
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The social and nonsocial conditions elicited a similar network, substantially stronger than those elicited by the scrambled versions.
source: Overall, the social and nonsocial conditions elicited a similar network, substantially stronger than those elicited by the scrambled versions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the activation patterns across conditions.

claim: The comparison of social with nonsocial condition revealed stronger activations in frontal, somatosensory, and cingulate cortex for the social condition.
source: To identify areas that were more active for the observation of social interactions, we compared the social with the nonsocial condition (Figure 2; see Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for individual analyses, cluster-defining threshold p<0.05, α = 0.05 for all contrasts). This analysis revealed stronger activations in frontal, somatosensory, and cingulate cortex for the social condition.
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI contrast analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Significant differences between social and nonsocial conditions were present in frontal areas 10, 9, 14c, 14r, 45, 46d, 47L, 8ad, 8b, 8av, 8C, 6av, 6bv, and 6DC.
source: Significant differences were present in frontal areas 10, 9, 14c, 14r, 45, 46d, 47L, 8ad, 8b, 8av, 8C, 6av, 6bv, and 6DC.
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI contrast analysis between social and nonsocial conditions.

claim: Somatosensory areas S2I, S2PV, S2PR, 1/2, 3a, and 3b, and motor areas 4ab and ProM were more active for the social than nonsocial condition.
source: More posteriorly, somatosensory areas S2I, S2PV, S2PR, 1/2, 3a, and 3b, and motor areas 4ab and ProM were more active for the social than nonsocial condition.
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI contrast analysis between social and nonsocial conditions.

claim: Activations in parietal areas (MIP, VIP), rostral temporal areas (STR, TPO, AuCPB, AuRPB), and cingulate areas (25, 23b, and 31) were observed for social vs. nonsocial comparison.
source: We also observed activations in parietal areas (MIP, VIP), rostral temporal areas (STR, TPO, AuCPB, AuRPB), and in cingulate areas (25, 23b, and 31).
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI contrast analysis between social and nonsocial conditions.

claim: The largest differences between social and nonsocial conditions were present in motor/premotor cortex at the border of areas 4ab and 6DC, at the border of somatosensory area 1/2 and premotor areas 6av and 6bc, and in area 25 and orbitofrontal area 14.
source: The largest differences were present in motor/premotor cortex at the border of areas 4ab and 6DC, at the border of somatosensory area 1/2 and premotor areas 6av and 6bc, and in area 25 and orbitofrontal area 14.
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI contrast analysis between social and nonsocial conditions.

claim: Differences between social and nonsocial interaction conditions are found at the subcortical level in the SC, Tha, Amy, and CeB.
source: Differences between social and single interaction conditions are also found at the subcortical level in the SC, Tha, Amy, and CeB.
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI contrast analysis between social and nonsocial conditions.

claim: Stronger activations for the nonsocial condition were mainly located in visual (V1, V2, V3, V4, V6), cingulate area 24b, and temporal areas (TF, TE2, TEO).
source: Stronger activations for the nonsocial condition were mainly located in visual (V1, V2, V3, V4, V6), cingulate area 24b, and temporal areas (TF, TE2, TEO).
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI contrast analysis between social and nonsocial conditions.

claim: Numerous activations looked very similar in both hemispheres but are less strong in the left hemisphere.
source: Overall numerous activations looked very similar in both hemispheres but are less strong in the left hemisphere (Figure 2; see Figure 2—figure supplement 2 for temporal signal-to-noise ratio maps).
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI data shown in Figure 2 and the tSNR maps.

claim: The interaction effect [social vs. social scrambled] minus [nonsocial vs. nonsocial scrambled] revealed most of the activations found by the social vs. nonsocial contrast but with less spread activations.
source: To better control for low-level visual features, we also reported the interaction effect [social vs. social scrambled] minus [nonsocial vs. nonsocial scrambled] (Figure 3; see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for individual analyses, cluster-defining threshold p<0.05, α = 0.05 for all contrasts). Overall, this analysis revealed most of the activations found by the previous contrast (Figure 2) but with less spread activations (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI interaction analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Significant interaction effect was present in frontal areas 10, 9, 14c, 45, 46d, 47L, 8ad, 8b, 8C, 6bv, and 6DC.
source: Significant interaction effect was present in frontal areas 10, 9, 14c, 45, 46d, 47L, 8ad, 8b, 8C, 6bv, and 6DC, and more posteriorly, in somatosensory areas S2I, S2PR, 1/2, 3a, and 3b, motor area 4ab, and rostral temporal areas (STR, TPO, AuCPB).
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI interaction analysis.

claim: The interaction effect showed activations in somatosensory areas S2I, S2PR, 1/2, 3a, and 3b, motor area 4ab, and rostral temporal areas (STR, TPO, AuCPB).
source: Significant interaction effect was present in frontal areas 10, 9, 14c, 45, 46d, 47L, 8ad, 8b, 8C, 6bv, and 6DC, and more posteriorly, in somatosensory areas S2I, S2PR, 1/2, 3a, and 3b, motor area 4ab, and rostral temporal areas (STR, TPO, AuCPB).
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI interaction analysis.

claim: The interaction effect showed activations in parietal area VIP, cingulate area 25, and at the subcortical level in the SC, Tha, Amy, and CeB.
source: We still observed activations in parietal areas (VIP), in cingulate area 25, and at the subcortical level in the SC, Tha, Amy, and CeB.
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI interaction analysis.

claim: No activation was observed in area 8aV in the interaction effect, indicating that the differences are not primarily related to saccades.
source: We did not observe any activation in area 8aV, indicating that the differences are not primarily related to saccades.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the absence of activation in a saccade-related area.

claim: Some areas showed stronger activation for the social condition than for the nonsocial condition (right area 25, right area 10, left area 10L, right area 14c, right area VIP, right area 6va, right area 6vb, right area 46d, left area 46d, and right area 45).
source: Some areas showed stronger activation for the social condition than for the nonsocial condition (paired t-tests, p<0.5; right area 25 p=0.0435; right area 10 p=0.0075; left area 10L p=0.0012; right area 14c p=0.0016; right area VIP p=0.0052; right area 6va p=0.027; right area 6vb p=0.021; right area 46d p=0.0186; left area 46d p=0.005; and right area 45 p=0.0291).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of ROI data shown in Figure 4.

claim: These areas (25, 10, 10L, 14c, VIP, 6va, 46d, 45) also showed stronger activations for the social condition than for its scrambled version, except for right area 6vb and left 46d.
source: These areas also showed stronger activations for the social condition than for its scrambled version (paired t-tests, p<0.05; right area 25 p=0.0355; right area 10 p=0.049; left area 10L p=0.011; right area 14c p=0.002; right area VIP p=0.0257; right area 6va p=0.038; right area 46d p=0.0074; and right area 45 p=2.8 10−6) except for right area 6vb and left 46d.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of ROI data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Other areas (left area 25, left area 6va, right area 8ad, left area 8ad, right area 8av, left area 8av, and left area 45) did not show significant difference between social and nonsocial conditions but showed stronger activations for the social conditions than for its scrambled version.
source: Other areas did not show significant difference between social and nonsocial conditions but stronger activations for the social conditions than for its scrambled version (paired t-tests, p<0.05; left area 25 p=0.027; left area 6va p=0.012; right area 8ad p=0.007; left area 8ad p=0.014; right area 8av p=6.9 10−6; left area 8av p=0.004; and left area 45 p=0.004).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of ROI data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Both the social and nonsocial conditions showed strong occipitotemporal activation when compared to their scrambled versions, consistent with the location of face and body patches.
source: Both the social and nonsocial conditions showed strong occipitotemporal activation when compared to their scrambled versions, consistent with the location of face and body patches.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fMRI data in the context of known face processing areas.

claim: The occipitotemporal activations in the intact vs. scrambled movies resemble face-selective patches previously found in marmoset fMRI studies using photos of marmoset faces and body parts or videos of faces.
source: The occipitotemporal activations in the intact vs. scrambled movies resemble face-selective patches previously found in marmoset fMRI studies using photos of marmoset faces and body parts (Hung et al., 2015) or videos of faces (Schaeffer et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with previous fMRI studies in marmosets.

claim: The occipitotemporal activations include the occipital (V2/V3), anterior dorsal (rostral TE), middle dorsal (caudal TE), posterior dorsal (FST), and posterior ventral (V4/TEO) face patches.
source: They include the occipital (V2/V3), anterior dorsal (rostral TE), middle dorsal (caudal TE), posterior dorsal (FST), and posterior ventral (V4/TEO) face patches.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fMRI data in the context of known face processing areas.

claim: The study confirmed a recent report of a frontal face patch located in the lateral frontal cortex (45/47L) in both the social and nonsocial condition.
source: We also confirmed a recent report of a frontal face patch located in the lateral frontal cortex (45/47L) in both the social and nonsocial condition (Schaeffer et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the current fMRI data and comparison with a previous study.

claim: Face processing areas are recruited independent of social interactions.
source: These areas are thus recruited for face processing independent of social interactions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that face areas are activated in both social and nonsocial conditions.

claim: Sliwa and Freiwald (2017) identified an exclusively social interaction brain network in macaques that included predominately frontal and cingulate areas.
source: Recently, Sliwa and Freiwald, 2017 identified an exclusively social interaction brain network in macaques using fMRI. This network included predominately frontal and cingulate areas (14, 24c, 25, 32, 9, 10, 8B, 8D, 46D, 46V, 47L, 47O, 44, 6VR [F5], 6DC [F2], ProM).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous fMRI study in macaques.

claim: The frontal areas identified in macaques for social interaction observation overlap well with the frontal areas found in marmosets for a similar comparison.
source: These overlap well with the frontal areas that we found here for a similar comparison in marmosets.
evidence: This is a comparison between the current marmoset data and previous macaque data.

claim: Strong right hemisphere activation was observed at the border of somatosensory area 1/2 and premotor areas 6av and 6bc and in the primary motor cortex 4ab in the marmoset.
source: In addition, we observed strong right hemisphere activation at the border of somatosensory area 1/2 and premotor areas 6av and 6bc and in the primary motor cortex 4ab in the marmoset.
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI data from marmosets.

claim: Area PG was activated in both social, social scrambled, and nonsocial condition but not during nonsocial scrambled version.
source: We also found activation of area PG (homologous with area 7a in macaque) in both social, social scrambled, and nonsocial condition but not during nonsocial scrambled version.
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI data from marmosets.

claim: In macaques, area PG/7a is strongly activated during social interaction observation but also showed, albeit weaker, activation during nonsocial interaction observation.
source: In macaques (Sliwa and Freiwald, 2017), area PG/7a is strongly activated during social interaction observation but also showed, albeit weaker, activation during nonsocial interaction observation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous fMRI study in macaques.

claim: In macaques, area PG contains motor neurons coding goal-directed motor acts.
source: In macaques, this area contains motor neurons coding goal-directed motor acts in macaques (Rozzi et al., 2008), which were present both in our social and nonsocial condition.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study on macaque area PG.

claim: The role of area PG is still poorly understood in marmosets, except that it seems to be a major functional hub of the marmoset brain.
source: The role of area PG is still poorly understood in marmosets, except that it seems to be a major functional hub of the marmoset brain (Ghahremani et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study on marmoset brain connectivity.

claim: Most of the areas activated by the social vs. nonsocial comparison form a strong structural network in marmosets.
source: Most of the areas activated by the social vs. nonsocial comparison (and present in the interaction effect [social vs. social scrambled] minus [nonsocial vs. nonsocial scrambled]) are already known to form a strong structural network in marmosets and many have been implicated in various aspects of social cognition in humans and macaques.
evidence: This is supported by existing knowledge of marmoset brain connectivity.

claim: Many of the areas activated by the social vs. nonsocial comparison have been implicated in various aspects of social cognition in humans and macaques.
source: Most of the areas activated by the social vs. nonsocial comparison (and present in the interaction effect [social vs. social scrambled] minus [nonsocial vs. nonsocial scrambled]) are already known to form a strong structural network in marmosets and many have been implicated in various aspects of social cognition in humans and macaques.
evidence: This is supported by existing knowledge of social cognition networks in primates.

claim: None of the oculomotor areas were activated by the social vs. nonsocial contrast, precluding any confounds with eye movements.
source: It should be noted that none of the oculomotor areas were activated by this contrast, precluding any confounds with eye movements.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the absence of activation in oculomotor areas.

claim: Eye movements, and particularly visual saccades, mostly activate the lateral intraparietal area (LIP) and the frontal eye field in primates.
source: Eye movements, and particularly visual saccades, mostly activate the lateral intraparietal area (LIP) and the frontal eye field in primates.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about oculomotor control in primates.

claim: Saccades can be evoked by electrical stimulation of areas 45, 8aV, 8C, and 6DR in marmosets.
source: Our group has mapped the saccade circuity in marmosets with multimodal approaches (electrophysiology and fMRI) (Ghahremani et al., 2017; Johnston et al., 2019; Schaeffer et al., 2019b; Selvanayagam et al., 2019). Together, this work demonstrates that saccades can be evoked by electrical stimulation of areas 45, 8aV, 8C, and 6DR.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous electrophysiology and fMRI studies in marmosets.

claim: Saccade-related regions (45, 8aV, 8C, 6DR) are activated in task-based fMRI with a visuomotor task and are functionally connected to the superior colliculus and other saccade-related regions.
source: These regions are also activated in task-based fMRI with a visuomotor task and are functionally connected to the superior colliculus and other saccade-related regions as shown with RS-fMRI.
evidence: This is supported by previous fMRI studies in marmosets.

claim: In the contrast between the social and nonsocial conditions, only a small portion of saccade-related areas was activated and only in the right hemisphere.
source: In our contrast between the social and nonsocial conditions, only a small portion of these areas was activated and only in the right hemisphere.
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI contrast analysis.

claim: In the interaction effect contrast, no activation was present in area 8aV and only weak activations were observed in the dorsal part of 8aD and 6DR.
source: In addition, in the interaction effect contrast, no activation was present in area 8aV and only weak activations were observed in the dorsal part of 8aD and 6DR, suggesting that the activations we observed in our contrast are not directly related to oculomotor areas and so preclude most of the confound with eye movements.
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI interaction analysis and used to infer lack of eye movement confounds.

claim: The PSC analysis of areas 8aV and 8aD showed no significant difference between social and nonsocial conditions.
source: Furthermore, the PSC analysis of areas 8aV and 8aD showed no significant difference between social and nonsocial conditions.
evidence: This is supported by the ROI analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Stimulation of area 45 evokes small saccades.
source: However, stimulation of area 45 evokes small saccades (Selvanayagam et al., 2019), and we observed here activation of the right area 45 in both social and nonsocial conditions as well as more activation for the social than nonsocial condition.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous electrophysiology study in marmosets.

claim: Right area 45 was activated in both social and nonsocial conditions as well as more activation for the social than nonsocial condition.
source: However, stimulation of area 45 evokes small saccades (Selvanayagam et al., 2019), and we observed here activation of the right area 45 in both social and nonsocial conditions as well as more activation for the social than nonsocial condition.
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI data.

claim: The social condition may have elicited more small saccades related to the exploration of the facial expression and the interaction itself compared to the nonsocial interaction.
source: The social condition may have elicited more small saccades related to the exploration of the facial expression and the interaction itself compared to the nonsocial interaction, which may involve more large explorations.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the area 45 activation.

claim: The animals were not rewarded for fixation or staying engaged during the task.
source: The animals were not rewarded for fixation or staying engaged during the task, and the quality of the video eye tracking did not allow us to confidently evaluate the animal's engagement/fixation across conditions and runs.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the experimental design.

claim: The quality of the video eye tracking did not allow confident evaluation of the animal's engagement/fixation across conditions and runs.
source: The animals were not rewarded for fixation or staying engaged during the task, and the quality of the video eye tracking did not allow us to confidently evaluate the animal's engagement/fixation across conditions and runs.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the experimental setup.

claim: Area 10 is densely connected with areas 14 and 9, to the temporal pole (STR) and parabelt auditory cortex.
source: Area 10 is densely connected with areas 14 and 9, to the temporal pole (STR) and parabelt auditory cortex (Buckner and Margulies, 2019; Burman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: Area 10 receives projections from parahippocampal, ventral somatosensory, and premotor areas.
source: Area 10 also receives projections from parahippocampal, ventral somatosensory, and premotor areas.
evidence: This is supported by existing knowledge of marmoset brain connectivity.

claim: Area 10 is a key node of a social cognition circuitry in humans.
source: It is a key node of a social cognition circuitry in humans (Simmons et al., 2010) and linked to areas integrating information about social attention, intentionality, and other's body actions in space in macaques (Jellema et al., 2000; Nummenmaa and Calder, 2009; Oram and Perrett, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study on human social cognition.

claim: Area 10 is linked to areas integrating information about social attention, intentionality, and other's body actions in space in macaques.
source: It is a key node of a social cognition circuitry in humans (Simmons et al., 2010) and linked to areas integrating information about social attention, intentionality, and other's body actions in space in macaques (Jellema et al., 2000; Nummenmaa and Calder, 2009; Oram and Perrett, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on macaque social cognition.

claim: Area 10 is connected with area 25 in marmosets and macaques.
source: Area 10 is also connected with area 25 in marmosets (Burman et al., 2011) and macaques (Joyce and Barbas, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: Connections of area 25 with the amygdala, ventral striatum, hypothalamus, and periaqueductal gray, as well as with the anterior insula in macaques suggest a role of area 25 in emotion, visceromotor functions, and memory.
source: Connections with the amygdala, ventral striatum, hypothalamus, and periaqueductal gray, as well as with the anterior insula in macaques suggest a role of area 25 in emotion, visceromotor functions, and memory (Alexander et al., 2020; Alexander et al., 2019; Joyce and Barbas, 2018; Öngür et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous anatomical and functional studies.

claim: The social condition videos showed marmosets playing or grooming each other, which may have triggered emotions and activated memories in the animals.
source: Our videos for the social condition showed marmosets playing or grooming each other, which may have triggered emotions and activated memories in the animals.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of why area 25 was activated.

claim: Tracer studies of area 14 in marmosets have shown connections with amygdala, thalamus, and parahippocampal areas.
source: Tracer studies of area 14 in marmosets (Burman and Rosa, 2009), and some tracing data of the orbitofrontal cortex, encompassing area 14, have shown connections with amygdala, thalamus, and parahippocampal areas (Roberts et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: Area 14 seems to play a crucial role for appetitive value, reward processing, and decision making in humans and in marmosets.
source: Area 14 seems to play a crucial role for appetitive value, reward processing, and decision making in humans (Elliott et al., 2010; FitzGerald et al., 2009) and in marmosets (Roberts and Wallis, 2000; Roberts and Clarke, 2019; Stawicka et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous functional studies in humans and marmosets.

claim: Lesions in area 14 have been associated with social and emotional disturbance in humans.
source: Lesions in this area have been associated with social and emotional disturbance in humans (Bechara et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous lesion study in humans.

claim: Rostral area 14 provides a major input to area 9 and sends outputs to area 10.
source: Rostral area 14 also provides a major input to area 9 and send outputs to area 10 (Burman et al., 2011; Burman et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: Sliwa and Freiwald (2017) identified a parieto-premotor network involved in social interaction analysis that included the posterior part of area AIP and premotor area F5.
source: Sliwa and Freiwald, 2017 also identified a parieto-premotor network involved in social interaction analysis. This network included the posterior part of area AIP and premotor area F5 that have been shown to contain mirror neurons in macaques (Cléry et al., 2015; Cléry and Hamed, 2018; Rizzolatti et al., 1996; Rizzolatti and Fogassi, 2014; Rizzolatti and Matelli, 2003; Rizzolatti and Rozzi, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous fMRI study in macaques and citations to mirror neuron studies.

claim: Area AIP and premotor area F5 have been shown to contain mirror neurons in macaques.
source: This network included the posterior part of area AIP and premotor area F5 that have been shown to contain mirror neurons in macaques (Cléry et al., 2015; Cléry and Hamed, 2018; Rizzolatti et al., 1996; Rizzolatti and Fogassi, 2014; Rizzolatti and Matelli, 2003; Rizzolatti and Rozzi, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous electrophysiology studies in macaques.

claim: The literature suggests a role for the AIP/F5 mirror system in recognizing and understanding other agent's intention and action.
source: This literature, in addition to the study of Sliwa and Freiwald, 2017, suggests a role for this mirror system in recognizing and understanding other agent's intention and action.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the mirror neuron literature and the Sliwa and Freiwald study.

claim: In the macaque study by Sliwa and Freiwald (2017), the AIP/F5 network also responded to physical interactions between objects, suggesting a broader role for this network.
source: However, in this macaque study (Sliwa and Freiwald, 2017), this AIP/F5 network also responded to physical interactions between objects (not tested here), suggesting a broader role for this network.
evidence: This is supported by citation to the Sliwa and Freiwald study.

claim: Areas AIP and F5 were activated by the observation of nonsocial (i.e., 'agent-object interaction') and social interactions (i.e., 'agent-agent interaction') in marmosets.
source: Here, we found that these areas were activated by the observation of nonsocial (i.e., 'agent-object interaction') and social interactions (i.e., 'agent-agent interaction') in marmosets.
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI data from marmosets.

claim: The mirror neuron system is still poorly understood in marmosets.
source: The mirror neuron system is still poorly understood in marmosets; however, neurons with characteristic 'mirror' properties have been identified in the superior temporal sulcus and in area 6V in marmosets (Suzuki et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as current knowledge about marmoset neuroscience.

claim: Neurons with characteristic 'mirror' properties have been identified in the superior temporal sulcus and in area 6V in marmosets.
source: The mirror neuron system is still poorly understood in marmosets; however, neurons with characteristic 'mirror' properties have been identified in the superior temporal sulcus and in area 6V in marmosets (Suzuki et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous electrophysiology study in marmosets.

claim: The contrast between the social and nonsocial condition revealed strong activations of parietal areas MIP and VIP in addition to premotor area 6V.
source: Interestingly, the contrast between the social and nonsocial condition also revealed strong activations of parietal areas MIP and VIP in addition to premotor area 6V (corresponding to areas F4 and F5 in macaques, see Matelli et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI contrast analysis.

claim: Premotor area 6V in marmosets corresponds to areas F4 and F5 in macaques.
source: Interestingly, the contrast between the social and nonsocial condition also revealed strong activations of parietal areas MIP and VIP in addition to premotor area 6V (corresponding to areas F4 and F5 in macaques, see Matelli et al., 1985).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous anatomical study.

claim: A parieto-frontal network related to VIP and F4 has been suggested to contribute to the construction of both the representation of one own's body and of the body of others in macaques.
source: A parieto-frontal network related to VIP and F4 has been suggested to contribute to the construction of both the representation of one own's body and of the body of others in macaques (Cléry et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous review.

claim: Both areas VIP and F4 are strongly linked to peripersonal space representation, defense, avoidance behavior, and social cognition.
source: Both areas VIP and F4 are strongly linked to peripersonal space representation, defense, avoidance behavior, and social cognition (Brozzoli et al., 2013; Cléry et al., 2018; Cléry et al., 2017; Ishida et al., 2010; for review, see Cléry et al., 2015; Cléry and Hamed, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on VIP and F4 function.

claim: Areas VIP and 6V contribute to social interaction analysis in marmosets.
source: Our current study suggests that areas VIP and 6V also contribute to social interaction analysis in marmosets.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the current fMRI data.

claim: Strong activations of somatosensory (1/2, 3a, 3b, SII) and motor areas (4ab, PGM) were found in marmosets but were absent in macaque monkeys.
source: Even though the monkeys were simply watching other marmosets interacting with other marmosets or objects, we also found strong activations of somatosensory (1/2, 3a, 3b, SII) and motor areas (4ab, PGM) that were absent in macaque monkeys (Sliwa and Freiwald, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the current fMRI data and comparison with the macaque study.

claim: Activations in somatosensory and motor areas were localized in areas that are also activated by tactile stimulation of the face and arm.
source: Activations were localized in areas that are also activated by tactile stimulation of the face and arm (Cléry et al., 2020), body parts where tactile stimulation would often occur during social interactions (grooming, playing).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous somatosensory mapping study in marmosets.

claim: SII was activated in both hemispheres during social interaction observation.
source: Particularly SII (Cléry et al., 2020; Huffman and Krubitzer, 2001; Krubitzer and Kaas, 1990; H-x et al., 2002) was activated in both hemispheres.
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI data and citations to previous SII studies.

claim: A role of SII in social interaction processing is consistent with its involvement in the observation of others' actions, as demonstrated by human and macaque studies.
source: A role of SII in social interaction processing is consistent with its involvement in the observation of others' actions, as demonstrated both by human (Keysers et al., 2004; Blakemore et al., 2005; Lee Masson et al., 2018; for reviews, see Keysers et al., 2010; Bretas et al., 2020) and macaque studies (Hihara et al., 2015; Raos et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on SII function in action observation.

claim: The data showed stronger activations in the right hemisphere compared to the left hemisphere.
source: Our data showed stronger activations in the right hemisphere compared to the left hemisphere, even if the overall pattern looked similar.
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI data.

claim: The temporal signal-to-noise ratio (tSNR) map showed a slightly lower tSNR in the left hemisphere, which may have led to the difference of activation observed.
source: The temporal signal-to-noise ratio (tSNR) map showed a slightly lower tSNR in the left hemisphere (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), which may have led to the difference of activation we observed.
evidence: This is supported by the tSNR map shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The difference in activation between hemispheres may be due to a real lateralization effect during social behaviors.
source: However, this difference may also be due to a real lateralization effect during social behaviors.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation for the hemispheric differences.

claim: The right hemisphere has a relative advantage over the left hemisphere in identifying social stimuli, understanding the intentions of others, social relationships, and social interactions in humans.
source: Indeed, it has been shown that the right hemisphere has a relative advantage over the left hemisphere, particularly in identifying social stimuli, understanding the intentions of others, social relationships, and social interactions in humans (see review, Hecht, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review on hemispheric lateralization in humans.

claim: The data may reflect a similar lateralization for social processing in marmosets as observed in humans.
source: Consequently, our data may reflect a similar lateralization for social processing in marmosets.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the hemispheric differences.

claim: Deactivation was observed in both the social and nonsocial condition that were not present during the scrambled versions.
source: An interesting finding with our current study is the deactivation observed in both the social and nonsocial condition that were not present during the scrambled versions.
evidence: This is supported by the fMRI data.

claim: The deactivation may have been triggered by an expectation of hearing vocalizations that were not met.
source: This deactivation may have been triggered by an expectation of hearing vocalizations that were not met, but the actions during nonsocial interaction were mainly associated with eating so there is not necessarily vocalization associated with this kind of action.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the deactivation, with a caveat.

claim: The deactivation in both interaction conditions and not in the scrambled conditions may be the result of the marmosets' interest and engagement during the videos.
source: However, the fact that we observed this deactivation in both interaction conditions and not in the scrambled conditions may be the result of the marmosets' interest and engagement during the videos.
evidence: This is an alternative speculative interpretation of the deactivation.

claim: Looking at conspecifics interacting with each other or with their environment is more entertaining than blurred videos.
source: Looking at conspecifics interacting with each other or with their environment is more entertaining than blurred videos.
evidence: This is a reasonable inference about marmoset preferences.

claim: The study identified the neural circuitry for social interaction observation in marmosets that resembles the one identified in Old World macaque monkeys.
source: In summary, we have identified the neural circuitry for social interaction observation in marmosets that resembles the one identified in Old World macaque monkeys (Sliwa and Freiwald, 2017).
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the fMRI data and comparison with the macaque study.

claim: Old and New World primates separated ~40 million years ago.
source: As Old and New World primates separated ~40 million years ago, this suggests that neural circuits involved in social interaction observation are conserved between macaques and marmosets or may be the result of convergent evolution (they may have underwent similarities in selection pressure but also show differences in their social behavior; Preuss, 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about primate evolution.

claim: Neural circuits involved in social interaction observation are conserved between macaques and marmosets or may be the result of convergent evolution.
source: As Old and New World primates separated ~40 million years ago, this suggests that neural circuits involved in social interaction observation are conserved between macaques and marmosets or may be the result of convergent evolution (they may have underwent similarities in selection pressure but also show differences in their social behavior; Preuss, 2019).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the similarity of networks and evolutionary history, with citation.

claim: Social interaction observation recruited multiple brain networks, at both the cortical and subcortical levels, likely involved in emotion and affective processing, memory, peripersonal space representation, and the mirror neuron system.
source: Social interaction observation recruited multiple brain networks, at both the cortical and subcortical levels, likely involved in emotion and affective processing, memory, peripersonal space representation, and the mirror neuron system.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the fMRI data and known functions of activated areas.

claim: The identification of a preserved cortical and subcortical circuitry involved in social interaction observation in marmosets provides the map for studying the neural processes underlying primate social cognition.
source: Overall, the identification of a preserved cortical and subcortical circuitry involved in social interaction observation in marmosets provides the map for studying the neural processes underlying primate social cognition.
evidence: This is the concluding statement about the significance of the findings.

claim: All experimental methods were performed in accordance with the guidelines of the Canadian Council on Animal Care policy and an ethics protocol approved by the Animal Care Committee of the University of Western Ontario.
source: All experimental methods described were performed in accordance with the guidelines of the Canadian Council on Animal Care policy on the care and use of experimental animals and an ethics protocol #2017-114 approved by the Animal Care Committee of the University of Western Ontario.
evidence: This describes the ethical approval for the study.

claim: Three common marmosets (one female, two males) completed this study.
source: Three common marmosets (C. jacchus) completed this study (one female, two males).
evidence: This describes the subjects used in the study.

claim: The ages and weights of the marmosets at the time of the experiment were 30 months and 363 g (M1), 38 months and 410 g (M2), and 35 months and 310 g (M3).
source: Their ages and weights at the time of the experiment were 30 months and 363 g (M1), 38 months and 410 g (M2), and 35 months and 310 g (M3), respectively.
evidence: This describes the characteristics of the subjects.

claim: The animals were prepared for awake fMRI experiments by implanting an MRI-compatible head restraint/recording chamber.
source: The animals were prepared for awake fMRI experiments by implanting an MRI-compatible head restraint/recording chamber (for details, see Johnston et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the surgical preparation for the study.

claim: Each animal was initially habituated to the MRI environment over the course of 3 weeks.
source: Each animal was initially habituated to the MRI environment over the course of 3 weeks.
evidence: This describes the training procedure for the study.

claim: The habituation included acclimatization to the animal holder, the head-fixation system, and periodic sounds produced by the MRI sequences.
source: This included the acclimatization to the animal holder (tube closed by neck and tail plates), the head-fixation system, and periodic sounds produced by the MRI sequences (for details, see Schaeffer et al., 2019a).
evidence: This describes the training procedure for the study.

claim: The behavior of the animals was monitored throughout the training to assess the tolerance and well-being of the marmosets.
source: The behavior of the animals was monitored throughout the training to assess the tolerance and well-being of the marmosets (Silva et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the monitoring procedure during training.

claim: For MRI acquisition, the animal was placed in the sphinx position in an animal holder consisting of an MRI-compatible restraint system.
source: For MRI acquisition, the animal was placed in the sphinx position in an animal holder consisting of an MRI-compatible restraint system (Schaeffer et al., 2019a).
evidence: This describes the setup for MRI acquisition.

claim: The animal was first restrained using neck and tail plates, then the head was restrained by the fixation of the head chamber to the five-channel receive coil.
source: The animal was first restrained using neck and tail plates, then the head was restrained by the fixation of the head chamber to the five-channel receive coil.
evidence: This describes the restraint procedure for MRI acquisition.

claim: An MRI-compatible camera was positioned in front of the animal holder to allow monitoring of the animals during the acquisition sessions by a veterinary technician.
source: An MRI-compatible camera (model 12M-i, 60 Hz sampling rate, MRC Systems GmbH, Heidelberg, Germany) was positioned in front of the animal holder to allow monitoring of the animals during the acquisition sessions by a veterinary technician.
evidence: This describes the monitoring setup during MRI acquisition.

claim: The camera and the setup did not allow a proper recording of eye movements as the pupil signal was frequently lost.
source: However, this camera and the setup did not allow a proper recording of eye movements as the pupil signal was frequently lost.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the eye tracking setup.

claim: In the MR scanner, the animal faced a translucent plastic screen placed at the front of the bore (119 cm from the animal's head) where visual stimuli were displayed via back-projection after being reflected off of a first-surface mirror.
source: In the MR scanner, the animal faced a translucent plastic screen placed at the front of the bore (119 cm from the animal's head) where visual stimuli were displayed via back-projection after being reflected off of a first-surface mirror.
evidence: This describes the visual stimulus presentation setup.

claim: Images were projected with a SONY VPL-FE40 projector.
source: Images were projected with a SONY VPL-FE40 projector.
evidence: This describes the equipment used for stimulus presentation.

claim: The maximum visual angle from the center to the side of the screen was 6.5°.
source: The maximum visual angle from the center to the side of the screen was 6.5°.
evidence: This describes the visual field covered by the stimulus presentation.

claim: Stimuli were presented via Keynote and launched in synchronization with MRI TTL pulse triggers via a custom-written program running on a Raspberry Pi.
source: Stimuli were presented via Keynote (version 10.1, Apple Incorporated, CA) and launched in synchronization with MRI TTL pulse triggers via a custom-written program running on a Raspberry Pi (model 3 B+, Raspberry Pi Foundation, Cambridge, UK).
evidence: This describes the software and hardware used for stimulus presentation.

claim: Real-world videos were chosen to maximize cognitive engagement.
source: We chose real-world videos to maximize cognitive engagement (Finn and Bandettini, 2020; Meer et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a methodological choice supported by citations.

claim: Videos were edited into 12 s clips using custom video-editing software (iMovie).
source: Videos were edited into 12 s clips using custom video-editing software (iMovie, Apple Incorporated).
evidence: This describes the video preparation procedure.

claim: Two video clips were displayed within a block (6 s each), and 20 different videos clips were used in total.
source: Two video clips were displayed within a block (6 s each), and 20 different videos clips were used in total.
evidence: This describes the stimulus presentation design.

claim: The videos within the same run were different between the two repetitions of the block condition but played following the same order.
source: The videos within the same run were different between the two repetitions of the block condition but played following the same order.
evidence: This describes the stimulus presentation design.

claim: Scrambled versions of social interaction and nonsocial interaction videos were created by random rotation of the phase information using a custom program (MATLAB).
source: Scrambled versions of social interaction and nonsocial interaction videos (Figure 1b, d, right panel) were created by random rotation of the phase information using a custom program (MATLAB, The MathWorks, Matick, MA).
evidence: This describes the creation of scrambled control stimuli.

claim: To preserve motion and luminance components, the same random rotation matrix was used for each frame in the scrambled conditions.
source: To preserve motion and luminance components, the same random rotation matrix was used for each frame in the scrambled conditions.
evidence: This describes the method for creating scrambled stimuli.

claim: Videos were presented in the center of the screen (7° height × 13° width) during acquisition sequences.
source: Videos were presented in the center of the screen (7° height × 13° width) during acquisition sequences.
evidence: This describes the stimulus presentation parameters.

claim: Four pseudo-randomized conditions were each displayed twice following a block design.
source: These four pseudo-randomized conditions were each displayed twice (social condition, nonsocial condition, and scrambled versions of each) following a block design (Figure 5).
evidence: This describes the experimental design shown in Figure 5.

claim: Eight task condition blocks (12 s each) were separated by baseline blocks (18 s each) where a 0.36° circular black cue was displayed in the center of a gray background.
source: These eight task condition blocks (12 s each) were separated by baseline blocks (18 s each) where a 0.36° circular black cue was displayed in the center of a gray background.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Three different stimulus sets were used and counterbalanced within the same animal and between animals.
source: Three different stimulus sets were used and counterbalanced within the same animal and between animals.
evidence: This describes the counterbalancing procedure.

claim: A sequence lasted 253 s (4.3 min).
source: A sequence lasted 253 s (4.3 min).
evidence: This describes the duration of each experimental run.

claim: Motion and luminance varied across videos, mainly due to where the action took place.
source: As motion and luminance varied across videos, mainly due to where the action took place, we counterbalanced these differences across the selected videos, conditions, and order of presentation to avoid any link with the condition block itself.
evidence: This describes a potential confound and how it was addressed.

claim: No reward was provided to the monkeys during the scan session.
source: No reward has been provided to the monkeys during the scan session.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Data acquisition was performed using a 9.4 T, 31 cm horizontal-bore magnet with Bruker BioSpec Avance III HD console.
source: We performed data acquisition using a 9.4 T, 31 cm horizontal-bore magnet (Varian/Agilent, Yarnton, UK) and Bruker BioSpec Avance III HD console with the software package Paravision-6 (Bruker BioSpin Corp, Billerica, MA) at the Centre for Functional and Metabolic Mapping at the University of Western Ontario.
evidence: This describes the MRI equipment used.

claim: An in-house, custom-built integrated receive coil with five channels was used paired with a custom-built high-performance 15-cm-diameter gradient coil with 400 mT/m maximum gradient strength.
source: We used an in-house, custom-built integrated receive coil with five channels (Schaeffer et al., 2019a) paired with a custom-built high-performance 15-cm-diameter gradient coil with 400 mT/m maximum gradient strength (xMR, London, Canada; Peterson et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the MRI coils used.

claim: An in-house quadrature birdcage coil (12 cm inner diameter) was used for the transmit coil.
source: We used an in-house quadrature birdcage coil (12 cm inner diameter) for the transmit coil.
evidence: This describes the MRI transmit coil used.

claim: For each animal, a T2-weighted structural image was acquired to allow anatomical registration.
source: For each animal, a T2-weighted structural image was acquired, to allow an anatomical registration, with the following parameters: repetition time (TR) = 5500 ms; echo time (TE) = 53 ms; field of view (FOV) = 51.2 × 51.2 mm; voxel size = 0.133 × 0.133 × 0.5 mm; number of slices = 42 (axial); bandwidth = 50 kHz; GRAPPA acceleration factor = 2.
evidence: This describes the structural MRI acquisition parameters.

claim: For functional imaging, gradient-echo-based, single-shot echo-planar images covering the whole brain were acquired over multiple sessions.
source: For functional imaging, gradient-echo-based, single-shot echo-planar images covering the whole brain were acquired over multiple sessions (TR = 1500 ms; TE = 15 ms; flip angle = 40°; FOV = 64 × 64 mm; matrix size = 128 × 128; voxel size = 0.5 mm isotropic; number of slices = 42 [axial]; bandwidth = 500 kHz; GRAPPA acceleration factor = 2 [anterior-posterior]).
evidence: This describes the functional MRI acquisition parameters.

claim: Monkey 1 performed 8 runs in four sessions, monkey 2 performed 11 runs in five sessions, and Monkey 3 performed 9 runs in four sessions.
source: Monkey 1 performed 8 runs in four sessions, monkey 2 performed 11 runs in five sessions, and Monkey 3 performed 9 runs in four sessions.
evidence: This describes the data collection for each subject.

claim: Eight runs per monkey were selected to have the same number of runs across subjects for the group analysis.
source: We selected eight runs per monkeys to have the same number of runs across subjects for the group analysis (the selection was based on the best engagement of the animal as assessed by visual monitoring during the sessions).
evidence: This describes the data selection procedure for analysis.

claim: Time series were preprocessed using AFNI, FSL, and ANTS software.
source: Time series were preprocessed using AFNI (Cox, 1996), FSL (Smith et al., 2004), and ANTS software (Advanced Normalization Tools, Avants et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the software used for data preprocessing.

claim: Raw functional images were converted to NifTI format using dcm2niix and reoriented from the sphinx position using FSL.
source: Raw functional images were converted to NifTI format using dcm2niix (Li et al., 2016) and reoriented from the sphinx position using FSL.
evidence: This describes the initial preprocessing steps.

claim: The images were despiked and volume registered to the middle volume of each time series.
source: The images were then despiked (AFNI's 3dDespike) and volume registered to the middle volume of each time series (AFNI's 3dvolreg).
evidence: This describes the preprocessing steps.

claim: Images were smoothed by a 1.5 mm full-width at half-maximum Gaussian kernel to reduce noise.
source: Images were smoothed by a 1.5 mm full-width at half-maximum Gaussian kernel to reduce noise (AFNI's 3dmerge).
evidence: This describes the spatial smoothing applied.

claim: An average functional image was calculated for each session and linearly registered to each animal's T2-weighted image.
source: An average functional image was then calculated for each session and linearly registered (FSL's FLIRT) to each animal's T2-weighted image – the 4D time-series data was carried over using this transformation matrix.
evidence: This describes the registration procedure.

claim: Anatomical images were manually skull-stripped, and this mask was applied to the functional images in anatomical space.
source: Anatomical images were manually skull-stripped, and this mask was applied to the functional images in anatomical space.
evidence: This describes the skull-stripping procedure.

claim: The T2-weighted images were nonlinearly registered to the NIH marmoset brain atlas using Advanced Normalization Tools.
source: The T2-weighted images were then nonlinearly registered to the NIH marmoset brain atlas (Liu et al., 2018) using Advanced Normalization Tools and the resultant transformation matrices stored for later transformation (see below).
evidence: This describes the normalization to atlas space.

claim: The olfactory bulb was manually removed from the T2-weighted images of each animal prior to registration as it was not included in the template image.
source: The olfactory bulb was manually removed from the T2-weighted images of each animal prior to registration as it was not included in the template image.
evidence: This describes a preprocessing step for registration.

claim: The task timing was convolved to the hemodynamic response, and a regressor was generated for each condition to be used in a regression analysis for each run.
source: The task timing was convolved to the hemodynamic response (using AFNI's 'BLOCK' convolution), and a regressor was generated for each condition to be used in a regression analysis (AFNI's 3dDeconvolve) for each run.
evidence: This describes the statistical modeling procedure.

claim: All four conditions were entered into the same model, along with polynomial detrending regressors, bandpass regressors, and the motion parameters.
source: All four conditions were entered into the same model, along with polynomial (N = 5) detrending regressors, bandpass regressors, and the motion parameters derived from the volume registration described above (these nuisance regressors correspond to the baseline variance for the statistical analysis model).
evidence: This describes the statistical modeling procedure.

claim: The resultant regression coefficient maps were registered to template space using the transformation matrices.
source: The resultant regression coefficient maps were then registered to template space using the transformation matrices described above.
evidence: This describes the transformation to template space.

claim: The T-value maps for each monkey were compared at the individual level via paired-sample t-tests and fixed effect analyses across the eight runs for each marmoset.
source: The T-value maps for each monkey were then compared at the individual level via paired-sample t-tests and fixed effect analyses across the eight runs for each marmoset (AFNI's 3dttest++) and at the group level via a three-way analysis of variance and mixed effect analysis (AFNI's 3danova3) using eight runs per marmosets (for a total of 24 runs).
evidence: This describes the statistical analysis procedure.

claim: At the group level, a three-way analysis of variance and mixed effect analysis was performed using eight runs per marmoset (for a total of 24 runs).
source: The T-value maps for each monkey were then compared at the individual level via paired-sample t-tests and fixed effect analyses across the eight runs for each marmoset (AFNI's 3dttest++) and at the group level via a three-way analysis of variance and mixed effect analysis (AFNI's 3danova3) using eight runs per marmosets (for a total of 24 runs).
evidence: This describes the statistical analysis procedure.

claim: A cluster-size correction derived from Monte Carlo simulations was applied to the resultant t-test maps for α = 0.05.
source: To protect against false positives, a cluster-size correction derived from Monte Carlo simulations was applied to the resultant t-test maps for α = 0.05 (using AFNI's 3dClustsim).
evidence: This describes the multiple comparisons correction procedure.

claim: The contrast between the social and nonsocial condition as well as the interaction effect was compared to previous fMRI and electrophysiological studies performed in marmosets to check if the observed activations may be related to eye movements.
source: The contrast between the social and nonsocial condition as well as the interaction effect [social vs. social scrambled] minus [nonsocial vs. nonsocial scrambled] was compared to previous fMRI and electrophysiological studies performed in marmosets (Ghahremani et al., 2017; Johnston et al., 2019; Schaeffer et al., 2019b; Selvanayagam et al., 2019) to check if the observed activations may be related to eye movements.
evidence: This describes a validation procedure to rule out eye movement confounds.

claim: The resultant T-value maps are displayed on coronal sections or fiducial maps obtained with Caret using the NIH marmoset brain template.
source: The resultant T-value maps are displayed on coronal sections or fiducial maps obtained with Caret (Van Essen et al., 2001; http://www.nitrc.org/projects/caret/) using the NIH marmoset brain template (Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the visualization procedure.

claim: Coordinates are presented with respect to the anterior commissure.
source: Coordinates are presented with respect to the anterior commissure.
evidence: This describes the coordinate system used.

claim: The labeling refers to the histology-based atlas of Paxinos et al., 2011 for the cortical regions and to the atlas of Liu et al., 2018 for the subcortical regions.
source: The labeling refers to the histology-based atlas of Paxinos et al., 2011 for the cortical regions and to the atlas of Liu et al., 2018 for the subcortical regions (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 2, Figure 3).
evidence: This describes the anatomical labeling system used.

claim: Twelve regions of interest were defined based on the Paxinos et al., 2011 atlas to evaluate the difference in response magnitude between conditions.
source: Twelve regions of interest, areas 25, 10, 14c, VIP, PG, AIP, 6va, 6vb, 46d, 45, 8av and 8ad, were defined based on the Paxinos et al., 2011 atlas to evaluate the difference in response magnitude between conditions.
evidence: This describes the ROI analysis procedure.

claim: Masks of ROI regions were generated using AFNI's 3dcalc in the right or left hemispheres of the 'NIH_Marmoset_atlas_Paxinos_cortex'.
source: First, masks of these regions were generated using AFNI's 3dcalc in the right or left hemispheres of the 'NIH_Marmoset_atlas_Paxinos_cortex'.
evidence: This describes the ROI mask creation procedure.

claim: Time series were extracted for each condition from the resultant regression coefficient maps using AFNI's 3dmaskave.
source: Then, time series were extracted for each condition from the resultant regression coefficient maps using AFNI's 3dmaskave.
evidence: This describes the time series extraction procedure.

claim: The mean and standard errors were computed and paired t-tests were calculated using MATLAB after the data were tested for normality (Kolmogorov–Smirnov test).
source: The mean and standard errors were computed and paired t-tests were calculated using MATLAB (version 2018a) after the data were tested for normality (Kolmogorov–Smirnov test).
evidence: This describes the statistical analysis of ROI data.
